title: Inside the race between Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos for control of outer space
description:
The Atlantic writer Josh Tyrangiel says Musk and Bezos each want to colonize the moon, mine its resources and launch thousands more satellites. He says their only real competition is each other.

TERRY GROSS, HOST: This is FRESH AIR. I'm Terry Gross. The space race used to be waged between countries like the U.S. and Russia. Now the race to control outer space is being waged between two tech billionaires and their companies, Elon Musk's SpaceX and Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin. Bezos is, of course, famous for creating Amazon, buying The Washington Post and founding the cloud computing company Amazon Web Services. Elon Musk is famous for being the CEO of Tesla, buying Twitter and turning it into X, and founding Starlink, which manufactures and launches satellites. Musk was also appointed by President Donald Trump to run DOGE - the Department of Government Efficiency. Bezos and Musk each want to colonize the moon and turn space into a supply chain for Earth.My guest, journalist Josh Tyrangiel, writes that the two men hope to preserve human life from the specter of climate change and expand mankind's understanding of the universe. Both would also like to dominate a market that, unlike every other market they've previously conquered, has no ceiling and few established rules. Accomplishing the visions of either man would rely on creating giant data centers in space. Tyrangiel is a staff writer at The Atlantic and wrote the November cover story titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos."In the piece, he describes their visions for colonizing outer space, the technology they're developing and what it would mean to turn parts of the moon into businesses. The rivalry between Bezos and Musk is so powerful, Tyrangiel says, their only real competition is with each other. Tyrangiel is a former Washington Post columnist, where he covered AI. He also led the global newsrooms at Bloomberg, Vice and Time magazine. His latest book, "AI For Good," is about people finding ways to use AI that are fixing problems, not causing them.Josh Tyrangiel, welcome to FRESH AIR. So these space colonization efforts are being led by billionaires and their businesses. I know Bezos and Musk love the idea of space exploration. And they're taking big financial risks. But they also stand to make huge profits and have great power. And their investors stand to lose money or profit, too. But what does it mean that something with such big implications for the future of mankind and for the future of our planet and outer space that these efforts are being led by private enterprise and not the U.S. government?JOSH TYRANGIEL: It's a great question. And it really goes to the heart of this very strange moment we're in. And space is a part of it, right? So in the early 2000s, the United States government made a policy decision, which basically opened up space to commercial development. There was a notion that the government itself was slow, expensive. Its development processes for rockets, for satellites, for all sorts of things were just not going to be competitive with private enterprise. And so we invited these private enterprises in. And at that point, it was really hard to know what the outcome would be.Jeff Bezos, in 2001, started Blue Origin. But, you know, many people described it to me as much more of a think tank or a science experiment for its first decade. SpaceX was kind of almost founded, you know, impetuously. It was a pirate ship, as one person described it to me. And really, they didn't know what their plan was other than to launch things into space. The Commercial Space Act allowed all of this activity to happen. And even people who are really critical of Bezos and Musk believe that it was the right call, believe that the degree of space activity we have - economic activity, research activity - would never have been achieved without opening this up.At the same time, without governance over it, what you get is a situation where one or two people properly capitalized can, first, take over a market. So it's sort of stunning how successful Elon Musk has been in space. I mean, one stat that just floored me is that in 2025, SpaceX launched about 80% of the things in orbit, 80%. And its next closest competitor was not Jeff Bezos. It was the government of China. So you have an individual controlling a company. And essentially, he has supranational capabilities. And what we discovered is that when you outsource that capability to an individual, you're at the mercy of their whims.And so, as far back as the early 2000s, I had sources talk to me about this notion within the Air Force of people calling it the mercurial billionaire problem. And they could foresee that down the road, if one person or a handful of people had properly capitalized their space businesses, there was nothing preventing them from doing what they wanted to do. We briefly saw an example of this when President Trump and Elon Musk were sort of post-DOGE feuding. And Musk said that he was no longer going to produce the rocket that could take Americans to the International Space Station. And he was going to cancel flights.And if he did that, we would have no way to get Americans to the space station domestically. What we would've had to do was pay $80 million to a Russian rocket to put an American on it to get it to the space station. And so when you lose that capability as a country, when you outsource it to an individual or, potentially, two individuals, you have to ask yourself, what risks do we incur? What governance did we not perform to get into this situation?GROSS: So what role does NASA play now?TYRANGIEL: So NASA still has a very important role in dictating American space policy. And, you know, the new administrator of NASA is a guy named Jared Isaacman. The people I spoke to really like him. They think that he's hard-charging. He believes and has set the mission that we're going to go to the moon, and Americans are going to get to the moon, and maybe SpaceX will make the lander that takes astronauts there, and maybe Blue Origin will. And he's pitted the two in a kind of competition against one another.But NASA doesn't really oversee satellite activity. And there are 11,000 Starlink satellites in space, which is about two-thirds of the orbital objects in space owned by Elon Musk. And so he controls the newest, most agile technology when it comes to telecommunications and internet access. NASA doesn't really control that, nor does it really oversee it. So NASA has a role to play. But on the commercial side, there's just not a ton of governance. And there's no real movement toward getting more governance.GROSS: Well, would you compare the relationship that NASA had with private contractors to the relationship NASA has now to Musk and Bezos?TYRANGIEL: Listen, NASA has always invoked private industry to get its projects done. The Apollo missions, which we all laud and really, I think, in memory, think of as just American missions, you know, there were a lot of contractors that helped make those missions possible. And they really collaborated. Those contractors built different parts of the spacecraft, made different components inside the spacecraft, all under the authority of NASA, which directed the contracting in very specific ways.What we're seeing right now is that Jared Isaacman, for the Artemis program, has said, I'm having a bake-off. It'll either be Blue Origin that creates the booster and the rocket and the lander that gets to the moon, or it'll be SpaceX. And they're in competition. The money, frankly, is meaningful to both companies. But it's not bigger than their economic plans overall. A lot of people I spoke to suggested that one way for the government to exercise power over these companies would be to revert to the way NASA used to function and say, frankly, right now, Bezos and Blue Origin have a better landing plan for the moon. Many people I spoke to said it's pretty clear that their lander is superior.But SpaceX has a much bigger rocket that could potentially be the refueling station for the Blue Origin and lander. And there's a very simple, practical approach, which is to say, we're the United States and we want our contractors to work for us. We don't want to be held at their mercy. SpaceX, if you want to be part of this program, you'll build the refueling. Blue Origin, you focus on the lander. And all of us will get there together. Director Isaacman didn't speak to me for this piece. Many people speculated about how he's going to conduct the next couple of years as these companies, you know, continue to be in competition. But I think it's a pretty rational way to regain some measure of control over these companies.GROSS: Well, let's take a short break here. If you're just joining us, my guest is Josh Tyrangiel. He's a staff writer at The Atlantic, where he wrote the November cover story, titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos." We'll be right back after a break. This is FRESH AIR.(SOUNDBITE OF THE ACORN'S "LOW GRAVITY")GROSS: This is FRESH AIR. Let's get back to the interview I recorded yesterday morning with Josh Tyrangiel, a staff writer at The Atlantic. He wrote the November cover story about the race between Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos to conquer space. It's titled "Choose Your Overlord: Musk Vs. Bezos."They're planning on sending thousands more satellites into space. Musk's company, SpaceX, already has satellite communications networks. And Ukraine has relied on them during the war with Russia. The Starlink satellite network has provided internet connectivity for the Ukrainian military. And Ukraine now also uses SpaceX's more high-powered, military-grade satellite network, Starshield, which is controlled by the Pentagon. Yesterday, Ukraine's access to Starshield was restricted, leaving the country unprepared for yesterday's Russian attacks.Facing questions about who is responsible for the decision, Musk wrote this on his platform, X. Quote, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS." Unquote. Earlier in the war, Musk temporarily stopped Ukraine's access to Starlink, saying that Ukraine had violated Starlink's rule that it can be used for defensive military actions, but not offensive ones. I asked Josh Tyrangiel about what all this says about Musk's power.TYRANGIEL: Ordinarily, we have entrusted the future of our civilizations to people we elect to office. We now have folks with a tremendous amount of power over our future, particularly if you view the future as being partially in space. And we have to reckon with it, whether we walk it back, whether we split these companies up. Whatever the remedy is, I don't actually know. But I think you'll see more and more of these kinds of incidents the more you concentrate power and the better the tech gets.GROSS: There are laws governing the seas. There are no laws yet - right? - governing outer space. It's kind of first come, first owned?TYRANGIEL: Well, we have international treaties about the moon. And in those treaties, it is said that companies conducting their business in space are ultimately overseen by the countries of their origin. So the United States is actually responsible for the comportment of these companies as they make plans on the moon, as they attempt to put data centers in space. But as we've seen over the last 10 years, having a plan for governance and actually using that plan and changing the way companies react are two very different things. We could certainly use more space laws. We could certainly use more governance of pollution in space, plans in space. But it's not like we're absent remedies for this. We just haven't used them.GROSS: You mentioned pollution. I keep wondering, like, if we colonize the moon and build data centers to have the energy that would be needed in order to colonize the moon, and there's some kind of supply chain brin...
